pairs.question: Quo lapide dies felicior notari solet, ut apud Catullum legitur?
pairs.question_en: With what kind of stone is a luckier day customarily marked, as we read in Catullus?
pairs.derivation: The Roman custom of marking lucky days with a white pebble ('lapide... candidiore notat') — a proverbial practice attested across Latin literature. One-word answer verbatim.

pairs.source_text: hic, uelut in nigro iactatis turbine nautis lenius aspirans aura secunda uenit iam prece Pollucis, iam Castoris implorata
pairs.question: Quibus deis precibus imploratis nautis turbine iactatis aura secunda venit, ut Catullus scribit?
pairs.question_en: To which gods do sailors tossed in the storm address the prayers that bring the favoring breeze, as Catullus writes?
pairs.derivation: The Dioscuri as rescuers of storm-tossed sailors, invoked by name at sea — the practice itself (distinct from the votive dedication in c.4). Two-name answer verbatim.

pairs.source_text: dicit: sed mulier cupido quod dicit amanti, in uento et rapida scribere oportet aqua.
pairs.question: Ubi scribi oportet quod mulier cupido amanti dicit, ut est in illo Catulli dicto?
pairs.question_en: Where ought one to write what a woman says to her eager lover, according to Catullus' famous saying?
pairs.answer_en: On the wind and on running water.
pairs.derivation: The proverb of c.70: lovers' promises written on wind and water — quoted ever since as the emblem of unreliable vows. Short answer verbatim.

pairs.source_text: hoc ne ipsi accideret, patrui perdepsuit ipsam uxorem, et patruum reddidit Arpocratem.
pairs.question: Cuius dei nomine Catullus hominem ad silentium redactum significat, cum 'reddidit Arpocratem' dicit?
pairs.question_en: By the name of what god does Catullus signify a man reduced to silence when he says he 'made him a Harpocrates'?
pairs.derivation: Harpocrates, the Egyptian child-god shown with finger to lips, proverbial for enforced silence — evidence of the cult's currency at Rome (so too in c.102). The point is checkable and translatable.

pairs.source_text: CHOMMODA dicebat, si quando commoda uellet dicere, et insidias Arrius hinsidias... Ionios fluctus, postquam illuc Arrius isset, iam non Ionios esse sed Hionios.
pairs.question: Quid Arrius verbis perperam addebat, cum 'chommoda' pro 'commoda' et 'hinsidias' pro 'insidias' diceret?
pairs.question_en: What did Arrius wrongly add to his words when he said 'chommoda' for 'commoda' and 'hinsidias' for 'insidias'?
pairs.derivation: Misplaced aspiration as a social marker of speech: Arrius' hypercorrect h's turned even the Ionian sea 'Hionian'. The fact — that aspiration betrayed one's class and schooling — is cultural and survives translation; the quoted examples carry the point.

pairs.source_text: ODI et amo. quare id faciam, fortasse requiris. nescio, sed fieri sentio et excrucior.
pairs.question: Quid Catullus simul se facere sentit, nescius quare, in celeberrimo suo disticho?
pairs.question_en: What does Catullus feel himself doing at once, not knowing why, in his most famous couplet?
pairs.derivation: 'Odi et amo' — the most famous distich in Latin, proverbial for the torment of contradictory passion. Anchored to Catullus; two-word answer verbatim.

pairs.source_text: nam magus ex matre et gnato gignatur oportet, si uera est Persarum impia religio
pairs.question: Ex quo coniugio magus apud Persas gigni oportet, si vera est eorum religio, ut Catullus refert?
pairs.question_en: From what union must a magus be born among the Persians, if their religion is true, as Catullus reports?
pairs.answer_en: From a mother and her son.
pairs.derivation: The Greco-Roman ethnographic claim (also in Xanthus and Strabo) that Persian magi sprang from mother-son unions — 'Persarum impia religio'. Anchored to the Persians and their magi; short answer verbatim.

pairs.source_text: gratus ut accepto ueneretur carmine diuos omentum in flamma pingue liquefaciens.
pairs.question: Quid magus Persarum in flamma liquefacit, dum divos carmine veneratur, ut Catullus scribit?
pairs.question_en: What does the Persian magus melt in the flame while venerating the gods with chant, as Catullus writes?
pairs.derivation: Magian ritual as Romans understood it: the fatty omentum melted in the sacrificial flame while hymns are chanted. Ethnographic rite-fact stated verbatim; short answer.

pairs.source_text: NIL nimium studeo, Caesar, tibi uelle placere, nec scire utrum sis albus an ater homo.
pairs.question: Quid Catullus de Caesare scire se non curare profitetur?
pairs.answer: Utrum albus an ater homo sit.
pairs.question_en: What does Catullus profess not to care to know about Caesar?
pairs.answer_en: Whether he is a white man or a black one.
pairs.derivation: The proverbial idiom 'albus an ater' — not to know whether a man is white or black = to care nothing for him — hurled at Caesar himself. Anchored to Caesar + Catullus; short answer verbatim.

pairs.source_text: ZMYRNA mei Cinnae nonam post denique messem quam coepta est nonamque edita post hiemem, milia cum interea quingenta Hortensius uno
pairs.question: Post quot messes et hiemes Zmyrna Cinnae poetae denique edita est?
pairs.question_en: After how many harvests and winters was the Zmyrna of the poet Cinna finally published?
pairs.answer_en: After the ninth harvest and the ninth winter (nine years).
pairs.derivation: The nine-year gestation of Cinna's Zmyrna — the neoteric ideal of slow perfection, set against Hortensius' five hundred thousand verses in one span. Number answer verbatim.

pairs.source_text: at Volusi annales Paduam morientur ad ipsam et laxas scombris saepe dabunt tunicas.
pairs.question: Quibus piscibus annales Volusi laxas tunicas dabunt, ut Catullus praedicit?
pairs.question_en: To what fish will the Annals of Volusius furnish loose wrappers, as Catullus predicts?
pairs.derivation: The fate of bad books: waste paper for wrapping fish ('laxas scombris... tunicas') — a judgment that became proverbial (cf. Martial). Anchored to Volusius' Annales; one-word answer verbatim.

pairs.source_text: Zmyrna cauas Satrachi penitus mittetur ad undas, Zmyrnam cana diu saecula peruoluent.
pairs.question: Ad cuius fluminis cavas undas Zmyrna Cinnae penitus mittetur, ut Catullus vaticinatur?
pairs.question_en: To the deep waters of what river will Cinna's Zmyrna travel, as Catullus prophesies?
pairs.derivation: The Satrachus in Cyprus — the river of the Zmyrna/Adonis story, where the learned poem will be read for grey centuries. Anchored to the named poem; one-name answer verbatim.

pairs.source_text: PARVA mei mihi sint cordi monimenta ..., at populus tumido gaudeat Antimacho.
pairs.question: Quo epitheto Antimachus poeta apud Catullum notatur, quo populus gaudeat?
pairs.question_en: With what epithet is the poet Antimachus branded in Catullus, in whom the crowd may take its pleasure?
pairs.derivation: The Callimachean verdict on Antimachus of Colophon — 'tumidus', the byword for bloated epic against the small polished poem. Literary-culture judgment; one-word answer verbatim.

pairs.source_text: certe non tanto mors immatura dolori est Quintiliae, quantum gaudet amore tuo.
pairs.question: Cuius feminae mortem immaturam Calvus, Catulli sodalis, luxit?
pairs.question_en: The untimely death of what woman did Calvus, Catullus' companion, mourn?
pairs.derivation: Quintilia, Calvus' beloved (his elegies on her were famous), consoled by Catullus in c.96. Anchored to Calvus; one-name answer verbatim.

pairs.source_text: MVLTAS per gentes et multa per aequora uectus aduenio has miseras, frater, ad inferias, ut te postremo donarem munere mortis et mutam nequiquam alloquerer cinerem.
pairs.question: Quo modo vectus Catullus ad inferias fratris sui pervenit?
pairs.answer: Multas per gentes et multa per aequora.
pairs.question_en: By what journey did Catullus come to his brother's funeral rites?
pairs.answer_en: Borne through many peoples and over many seas.
pairs.derivation: The famous opening of c.101: the long journey over lands and seas to the brother's grave in the Troad — the most quoted funerary lines in Latin. Anchored to Catullus + frater; short answer verbatim.

pairs.source_text: nunc tamen interea haec, prisco quae more parentum tradita sunt tristi munere ad inferias, accipe fraterno multum manantia fletu
pairs.question: Quo more inferiae ad sepulcrum fratris Catulli traditae sunt?
pairs.question_en: By what custom were the funeral offerings presented at the grave of Catullus' brother?
pairs.answer_en: By the ancient custom of the ancestors.
pairs.derivation: The inferiae — the offerings owed to the dead — handed down 'prisco more parentum': Roman funerary religion at its most explicit. Anchored to the rite by name; short answer verbatim.

pairs.source_text: atque in perpetuum, frater, aue atque uale.
pairs.question: Quibus verbis Catullus fratrem mortuum in perpetuum salutat?
pairs.question_en: With what words does Catullus salute his dead brother forever?
pairs.derivation: 'Ave atque vale' — the canonical Roman farewell to the dead, closing c.101 'in perpetuum'; the phrase became the epitome of Latin funerary address. Short answer verbatim.

pairs.source_text: aduenio has miseras, frater, ad inferias, ut te postremo donarem munere mortis et mutam nequiquam alloquerer cinerem.
pairs.question: Quid Catullus ad sepulcrum fratris nequiquam alloquitur?
pairs.question_en: What does Catullus address in vain at his brother's tomb?
pairs.derivation: The dead as 'muta cinis' — the cremated remains that cannot answer — evidencing Roman cremation and the pathos of address to the ash. Anchored to the brother's grave; short answer verbatim.

pairs.source_text: MENTVLA conatur Pipleium scandere montem: Musae furcillis praecipitem eiciunt.
pairs.question: Quibus numinibus sacer est mons Pipleius, quem poetaster apud Catullum scandere frustra conatur?
pairs.question_en: To what divinities is the Piplean mount sacred, which the would-be poet in Catullus tries in vain to climb?
pairs.derivation: Pipla/Pimpleia in Pieria as the Muses' own mountain — climbing it stands for writing poetry, and the Muses pitchfork the intruder off. Shared literary geography; one-word answer verbatim.

pairs.source_text: AVFILENA, uiro contentam uiuere solo, nuptarum laus ex laudibus eximiis
pairs.question: Quae laus nuptarum ex laudibus eximia est, ut Catullus scribit?
pairs.question_en: What is the choicest praise of married women, as Catullus writes?
pairs.answer_en: To live content with one husband alone.
pairs.derivation: The univira ideal — the one-husband woman as the crown of wifely praise — a central Roman value (cf. epitaphs' 'uni nupta'). Stated verbatim; short answer.

pairs.source_text: CONSVLE Pompeio primum duo, Cinna, solebant Maeciliam: facto consule nunc iterum manserunt duo, sed creuerunt milia in unum singula.
pairs.question: Quotiens Pompeius consul factus erat, cum Catullus carmen de Maecilia ad Cinnam scripsit?
pairs.question_en: How many times had Pompey been made consul when Catullus wrote his poem about Maecilia to Cinna?
pairs.derivation: Dating by consulship: the epigram spans from Pompey's first consulship to 'facto consule nunc iterum' (his second, 55 BC). Pompey's two consulships are the checkable fact; anchored by name.

pairs.source_text: cur non diuitiis Croesum superare potis sit, uno qui in saltu tot bona possideat
pairs.question: Quis rex apud Catullum, ut in proverbio, divitiarum summarum exemplum est?
pairs.question_en: Which king stands in Catullus, proverbially, as the exemplar of supreme wealth?
pairs.derivation: Croesus of Lydia as the byword for riches ('diuitiis Croesum superare') — the shared proverb of wealth. One-name answer verbatim.

pairs.source_text: Hunc lucum tibi dedico consecroque, Priape, qua domus tua Lampsaci est quaque ... Priape. nam te praecipue in suis urbibus colit ora Hellespontia, ceteris ostriosior oris.
pairs.question: In qua urbe Hellespontia domus Priapi esse dicitur apud Catullum?
pairs.question_en: In what city on the Hellespont is the home of Priapus said to be, according to Catullus?
pairs.derivation: Lampsacus as the canonical cult-home of Priapus, whom the Hellespontine coast worships above all — shared religious geography. One-name answer verbatim.

pairs.source_text: nam te praecipue in suis urbibus colit ora Hellespontia, ceteris ostriosior oris.
pairs.question: Quae ora, Priapum praecipue colens, ceteris oris ostriosior est, ut Catullus canit?
pairs.question_en: What coast, the chief worshipper of Priapus, is richer in oysters than all other shores, as Catullus sings?
pairs.derivation: The oyster-beds of the Hellespont ('ostriosior') — a food-geography fact of the ancient table, fixed in the epithet. One-word answer verbatim.
